extracted.intended_audience: students and learners of analytic geometry and conic sections (introductory to intermediate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Elementary development and applications of the theory of poles and polars in the plane, with emphasis on conic sections (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola): definitions, equations, constructions, and classical theorems (diameters, tangents, Pascal, Brianchon, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — reciprocal system / pole and polar
rubrics_metrics.description: Two systems of points which are so related, that to each point of the one system there is a corresponding line of the other system, and to each point of the second system a corresponding line of the first system, are named a reciprocal system. The point and the line are named in reference to each other pole and polar, or reciprocal polars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also stated in coordinate form: the co-ordinates of a given point in one system and the variable co-ordinates of a line in the other are interchangeable in the equation expressing their relation. (Introductory definitional basis for all subsequent constructions and formulae.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 1 — Equation of reciprocity between a point and its polar
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the equation of reciprocity between a point and its polar: derive equations (14)/(15) expressing the polar of a point (x1,y1) with respect to a general conic ay^2 + bxy + cx^2 + dy + ex + f = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed derivation by combining equations of two lines through a point and eliminating parameters; final formulae given as (14) and (15). These express the polar line coefficients as functions of the point's coordinates and the conic's coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 2 — General equation of reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: General form: (a u + b t + c) y + (a'q u + b'q t + e') x + a u t + b' t u + e'' = 0 (equations 16/17) will express the polar of a point when coordinates of one system regarded constant and variables in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives general template for reciprocity; useful for matching a given line/point to polar/pole by coefficient comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 3 — Co-ordinates of the pole
rubrics_metrics.description: The co-ordinates (x1,y1) of the pole of a given polar line can be found by equating the given line with the polar-formula (14) or (16) and matching coefficients of like powers of variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method: treat the polar line equation as identical to the general polar expression and solve for the point coordinates; used repeatedly to compute poles from lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 4 — Polar of intersection passes through poles; conversely polars intersect in pole of joining line
rubrics_metrics.description: The polar of the point of intersection of two lines passes through the poles of these lines; conversely, the polars of two points intersect in the pole of the line joining these points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic verification via substituting coordinates; foundational incidence relation linking poles/polars and intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 5 — Motion duality theorem (line turning ↔ pole on straight line)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line turns round a fixed point, its pole describes a straight line which is the polar of the fixed point; conversely, if a point moves in a straight line, its polar turns round a fixed point, the pole of that straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from art. 4; interpret parallelism and points at infinity as limiting cases. Useful for understanding locus behavior under duality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 6 — Poles of parallel lines are collinear
rubrics_metrics.description: The poles of all straight lines that are parallel to the same straight line are in one and the same straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction via viewing parallel lines as meeting at a point at infinity; leads directly to the notion of diameters (loci of poles of a family of parallel chords).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 7 — Equation of a diameter (locus of poles of a family of parallel lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a family of lines represented by equation in which p is constant and q variable, the locus of the poles (a diameter) is found by equating this family with the general polar form; equation (22) is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives constructive algebraic formula for the diameter conjugate to a given direction (line). Used to compute diameters conjugate to given lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 8 — Centre of a system (concurrent diameters)
rubrics_metrics.description: All the diameters of a system intersect in the same point (the centre of the system), or are parallel to one another; center coordinates derived from setting arbitrary parameter p in diameter equation leading to system (23).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives condition and formulae for center coordinates; notes exception when denominator degenerates (degenerate conic case b^2 - 4ac = 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 9 — Equation of a diameter to a conic (second degree)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a line family (24) with p constant and g variable, equating coefficients with polar form yields diameter equation (25): (Qap + b) y + (bp + 2c) x + (d p + e) = 0, which is the diameter to the conic (13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit coefficient relationships to compute diameter conjugate to a given line parameter p; practical for analytic construction of conjugate diameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 10 — Criterion of conjugate diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: If the equation to any diameter is y = p x + q, the equation of the diameter conjugate to it has coefficients satisfying: bp + 2c over 2ap + b (explicit formula) and condition Z a p p' + b(pt + p') + 2c = 0 (equivalent form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides two equivalent algebraic tests (explicit ratio form and symmetric polynomial condition) to check or compute conjugate diameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 11 — Centre of a conic section
rubrics_metrics.description: From the general diameter equation, letting p arbitrary yields simultaneous linear equations 2a x + b y + d = 0 and b x + 2c y + e = 0 whose solution gives the coordinates of the centre; degeneracy when b^2 - 4ac = 0 noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard method to compute centre of conic from coefficients; connects with art. 8 general discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 12 — Equation of a tangent to a conic of second degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Given point of contact (x1,y1), the tangent may be written and reduced to polar form: (2a x1 + b y1 + d) y + (2c x1 + b y1 + e) x + d y1 + e x1 + 2 f = 0 (equation (27)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation shows tangent is parallel to the line conjugate to the diameter through the point; gives explicit tangent equation in terms of conic coefficients and contact point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 13 — Tangent as polar and point as pole
rubrics_metrics.description: The tangent at any point (x1,y1) of a conic section can be regarded as the polar of this point; conversely, the point is the pole of the tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocity verified by interchangeability of coordinates in equation (27). Fundamental conceptual identification simplifying many constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 14 — Polar parallel to conjugate diameter through the point
rubrics_metrics.description: The polar of a point (x,y), in reference to a conic, is parallel to the diameter which is conjugate to that diameter which passes through the point (x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A geometric relation linking polars and conjugate diameters; helpful for geometric reasoning about directions of polars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 15 — Three polar/tangent/chord incidence properties
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) The line joining the points of contact of two tangents to the same conic is the polar of the point of intersection of these tangents (chord of contact). (b) The point of intersection of two chords is the pole of the line joining the intersection points of the pairs of tangents at their extremities. (c) If the angular point of an angle moves on a straight line while the containing lines touch a conic, the chords of contact turn about the same point, the pole of the line on which the angular point moves; conversely if a chord turns about a fixed point the tangents at its extremities intersect in the polar of that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part is a direct corollary of art. 13 and earlier incidence theorems (arts. 4,5); used to construct poles/polars from tangents and chords and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 16 — Reciprocal polars: inscribed and circumscribed polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polygon is inscribed in a conic and tangents at its vertices form a circumscribed polygon, then the two polygons are reciprocal polars of one another: sides of one are polars of vertices of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct application of tangent=polar (art. 13) and chord-of-contact facts; used to derive dual polygon relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 17 — Pascal's and Brianchon's theorems via polars
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an inscribed hexagon, the three pairs of opposite sides produced meet at three points which lie on a straight line (Pascal). Dually: for a circumscribed hexagon the three diagonals joining opposite vertices pass through the same point (Brianchon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic derivation via polars: polars of intersection points are certain lines joining corresponding opposite vertices; combination and subtraction of polar equations yield collinearity and concurrency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 18 — Polar of the focus is the directrix
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parabola (and analogously for ellipse and hyperbola), the polar of the focus is the directrix; shown by substituting focus coordinates into polar formula and obtaining directrix equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example with parabola y^2 = 4 m x and application of (14) to verify the directrix arises as the polar of the focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 19 — Tangents at extremities of a focal chord meet at directrix
rubrics_metrics.description: If a chord is drawn through the focus and tangents are drawn at its extremities, these tangents will intersect in the directrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows immediately from art. 18 and property in art. 15(c) about chord-of-contact; a direct geometric consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 20 — Quadrilateral inscribed/circumscribed polar relations (four theorems)
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) If four pairs of opposite sides of an inscribed/circumscribed quadrilateral are produced to meet, the four intersection points lie on one line. (B) The four diagonals of the two quadrilaterals pass through the same point. (C) The point and line are a pole and polar relative to the conic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof proceeds by identifying polars of intersection points and combining their equations; generalizes the hexagon duality to quadrilaterals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 21 — Relationships among polars of intersections and diagonals
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quadrilateral ABCD inscribed in a conic, if pairs of opposite sides meet in M and L and diagonals meet in Q, then ML is the polar of the pole Q; MQ is the polar of the pole L; QL is the polar of the pole M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate demonstration using chosen axes and substitution into polar formulae; provides explicit equations for these polars (eqs. 42–44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 22 — Diagonals of circumscribed quadrilateral pass through intersections of opposite sides of inscribed one
rubrics_metrics.description: If a quadrilateral is inscribed and another circumscribed about the same conic, the diagonals of the circumscribed quadrilateral pass through the points of intersection of opposite sides of the inscribed one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from previous polars theorems: uses that certain lines are polars of given points so they must pass through corresponding poles/intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium 1 — Harmonic pole and polar
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a point in the plane of a conic a line is drawn to meet the curve and the polar of the given point, this line will be divided harmonically at the four points. This property gives the names harmonic pole and polar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as an important property (no demonstration given here); referenced to geometrical treatments in Davies’s edition of Hutton for proofs and further examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 23 — Normal via equal conjugate diameters (perpendiculars property)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a point P in an ellipse perpendiculars PG, PH are let fall on two equal conjugate diameters, then the diagonal of the parallelogram on PG, PH is normal to the ellipse at P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation uses choosing equal conjugate diameters as axes, computing polars and perpendiculars, and showing the perpendicular from P to the polar coincides with the diagonal PM; ties polar to normal direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art. 24 — Triangle with angle bisector normal: side passes through pole of normal (coordinate formula for pole)
rubrics_metrics.description: If in triangle ABC inscribed in a conic the line bisecting interior angle A is a normal to the curve, then the side BC opposite to the bisected angle passes through the pole of the normal. Coordinates of the pole when polar coincides with x-axis are given; applied to show BC passes through that pole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: compute pole coordinates by equating polar form with axis, set conic relative to normal and tangent axes, and combine side equations with conic equation to show coincidence with pole coordinates; explicit algebraic steps provided.
